title: Three letters, then a story told in order.
subtitle: Pausing before the story of Musa begins

row.title: stop and listen
sub: something is about to be shown

then: Surah Al-Qasas was revealed in Makkah, close in time to Ash-Shu'ara and An-Naml. It opens with three separate letters whose meaning is {idea}known to Allah{/idea}. Then comes the fullest telling of the story of Musa.
now: You have heard the Musa story since childhood. The basket, the river, the sea. Your thumb is ready to scroll past it. {idea}These letters are a speed bump.{/idea} Slow down, as if you were hearing it for the first time.
old: I already know this story, so I can skim it.
new: The opening letters ask me to stop and pay attention before anything else is said.
try: Before you read the next few verses, put your phone face down and read them once slowly.

title: A Book that makes things plain.
subtitle: What kind of book is speaking to you
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the Book is {idea}clear and makes plain the true reality of things{/idea}. It tells what happened and what will happen. This line frames the story that follows as truth, not legend.
now: Your feed is full of hot takes that contradict each other by lunchtime. Everyone has a version. {idea}Here is a source that claims to show things as they really are.{/idea} That is worth sitting with before deciding it is just old text.
old: Holy books are beautiful but hard to apply to real life.
new: This Book claims to make plain how things actually are, so I can test my life against it.
try: Pick one verse today and ask: what does this make clear about my situation right now?

title: Told in truth, for people ready to believe it.
subtitle: Who the Musa story is really for
then: Ibn Kathir links this to {idea}"We relate unto you the best of stories"{/idea}: Allah tells things as they really were, as if you were there seeing them. In Makkah, the Prophet ﷺ and his few followers were weak, and the powerful were mocking them.
now: You are the new person in the office, or the only one in the family who prays. The story of a powerful man and a weak people is not far away. {idea}It is told for you, to read as if you were standing in it.{/idea}
old: Stories of prophets are about them, not about me.
new: These stories are told for believers, so I am meant to see myself inside them.
try: As you read Musa's story this week, ask at each scene: who am I in this?

title: He split the people, then crushed one part.
subtitle: How a tyrant keeps control
then: Fir'awn was an arrogant tyrant who {trap}divided the people into classes{/trap} and forced the Children of Israel into hard labor night and day. He killed their sons out of fear that a boy among them would end his rule.
now: You do not need a throne to do a smaller version. The manager who plays staff against each other. The sibling who keeps the family split so they stay in charge. {trap}Divide, then lean on the weakest.{/trap} Notice if you ever feel safer when others are weaker.
old: Keeping people divided is just how you stay in control.
new: Splitting people and crushing the weakest is corruption, whatever the reason given.
try: Think of a group you are part of. Do one thing today that brings two sides closer, not further apart.

title: Allah wanted the crushed ones to lead.
subtitle: The plan above the tyrant's plan
then: While Fir'awn was crushing them, Allah says {reward}We wanted to confer favor{/reward} on the oppressed. Ibn Kathir notes this did happen, citing the verses where the weak people inherited the land.
now: You are the one with no seniority, the family with less money, the student everyone overlooks. It feels like the people at the top write the ending. {idea}The verse puts a different will above theirs.{/idea}
old: The people with power decide how my story ends.
new: Allah's will runs above the will of the powerful, and He can raise the overlooked.
try: Write down one situation where you feel powerless. Under it, write: Allah's will is above this.

title: What they feared came from the ones they crushed.
subtitle: Precautions against the decree of Allah

row.title: the decree
sub: when its term comes, no delay

then: Fir'awn hoped his strength would save him from Musa. Ibn Kathir says his precautions {trap}did not help him in the slightest{/trap}, because when Allah's term comes it cannot be delayed.
now: You check the weather app ten times, refresh the bank balance, rehearse every bad outcome. Some planning is wise. {trap}But some of it is trying to block Allah's decree.{/trap} That kind of control never works and wears you out.
old: If I plan hard enough, the thing I fear cannot happen.
new: I take sensible care, but no precaution overrides what Allah has decreed.
try: Name one worry you keep rechecking. Do one sensible step for it, then leave the rest with Allah.

title: Put him in the river, and do not be afraid.
subtitle: A mother told to let go with a promise

row.title: nurse, then the river
sub: do not fear, do not grieve

then: Boys born to the Children of Israel were being killed. Musa's mother lived by the Nile and {trap}was extremely scared for him{/trap}. It was inspired into her heart to nurse him and, when afraid, put him in a box on the river. Allah gave her {reward}a double promise{/reward}.
now: Your child leaves for university in another city. Your parent goes into surgery and the doors close. You cannot follow. {idea}Some things you have to place in the river{/idea}, trusting the One who controls where the water goes.
old: If I let go of what I love, I will lose it.
new: Letting go into Allah's care, with His promise, is not losing.
try: Think of someone you worry about. Make a short dua placing them in Allah's care, then say it once more tonight.

title: Fir'awn's family pulled their own downfall from the water.
subtitle: Raising the boy they were trying to prevent

row.title: servant women
sub: find a box in the Nile

then: The box floated past Fir'awn's house, and servant women carried it to his wife. Ibn Kathir notes this was so that {trap}he might become for them an enemy and a cause of grief{/trap}. The man killing boys would raise the one he feared.
now: You spent years avoiding something, and then it walks in through the door you held open. {idea}Allah's plans move through ordinary choices{/idea}, even the choices of people working against Him. Nothing is outside His reach.
old: People working against good can block what Allah intends.
new: Allah can carry out His plan through the very people trying to stop it.
try: Recall one time a door you dreaded led somewhere good. Thank Allah for it by name.

title: One woman's kindness saved the baby.
subtitle: Asiyah speaks up in Fir'awn's palace
then: When Fir'awn wanted to kill the child, his wife {reward}Asiyah bint Muzahim came to his defence{/reward}. She said he might benefit them. Ibn Kathir says he did: Allah guided her through him. Fir'awn said he was a comfort for her, not for him, and that was what happened.
now: A colleague is being pushed out and you are in the room. One sentence from you, "Let us not do this," could change it. {reward}You will not know what that small mercy grows into.{/reward} Asiyah did not know either.
old: Speaking up for someone weaker is not my business.
new: One merciful word in the wrong room can become the thing that saves me too.
try: Today, say one kind word in defence of someone who is not present to defend themselves.

title: Her heart was empty of everything but him.
subtitle: When grief nearly makes you blurt it out
then: Once the river took the box, she could think of nothing in the world but Musa. {trap}She almost told people{/trap} she had lost a son, which would have exposed him. Allah {idea}strengthened her heart{/idea} with patience.
now: You are in the hospital corridor waiting for news, or reading a message you dread. Your mind is blank except for one person. You might say things you regret. {idea}Steadiness in that moment is a gift you can ask for.{/idea}
old: If I fall apart in a crisis, I have failed as a believer.
new: Even a believer's heart can empty out; Allah is the One who holds it steady.
try: Next time panic rises, pause and say quietly: O Allah, hold my heart firm.

title: His sister followed quietly, eyes wide open.
subtitle: Doing your part while trusting the promise
then: His mother had Allah's promise, yet she sent her daughter to {idea}follow his traces{/idea}. Qatadah said the sister looked at him as if she was not really interested. No one noticed her.
now: You prayed for the job, and you also send the follow-up email. You trust Allah with your child, and you still check in. {idea}Trust is not doing nothing.{/idea} It is doing your part calmly, without panic.
old: If I truly trusted Allah, I would not need to do anything.
new: Trusting Allah's promise and quietly doing my part belong together.
try: Pick one thing you are praying about. Take one small practical step on it today.

title: He refused every nurse but one.
subtitle: A closed door that pointed the way home
then: Allah had {idea}forbidden all wet nurses for him{/idea}. The palace took him to the marketplace looking for anyone. His sister, unnoticed, offered a household that would care for him sincerely. When questioned, {reward}she answered wisely{/reward} and was let go.
now: Every application gets rejected. Every flat falls through. It feels like a wall. {idea}Sometimes the closing doors are a corridor{/idea}, steering you toward the one place you were meant to be.
old: When every option closes, something has gone wrong.
new: Allah may close many doors so that only the right one is left.
try: Think of one recent no. Ask Allah sincerely to show you the door it might be pointing to.

title: Back in her arms, and paid for it.
subtitle: The promise of Allah is true

row.title: the promise is true
sub: what you dislike can be good

then: Ibn Kathir says only {reward}a short time, a day and night or so{/reward}, passed between her distress and the way out. She nursed her own son at home and was paid for it. He cites {idea}"it may be that you dislike a thing which is good for you"{/idea}.
now: You remember the worst week of your life, the one you were sure would never end. Then something turned. {idea}Most people do not see the wisdom behind what happened{/idea}, but you can look back and notice it.
old: The hard thing that happened to me was only bad.
new: Allah's promise holds, and something I hated may have been carrying good.
try: Write down one hardship from your past and one good thing that came through it.

title: Strength and wisdom, given to the one who did good.
subtitle: Maturity as a gift, not just an age
then: Having told of his childhood, the story jumps to Musa as a grown man. Allah gave him {reward}judgement and knowledge{/reward}; Mujahid said this means prophethood. The verse ends with a rule: {idea}this is how Allah rewards those who do good{/idea}.
now: You are turning thirty, or forty, and expected to suddenly be wise. Birthdays do not do that. {idea}Clear judgement grows out of how you have been living{/idea}: the honest choices, the kindness no one saw.
old: Wisdom will come to me as I get older.
new: Allah gives judgement and knowledge as a reward for doing good, not just for getting older.
try: Do one good thing today purely for Allah and tell no one about it.

title: One blow in anger, and a man was dead.
subtitle: How fast a fight can go too far
then: Musa entered the city at a time when people were not paying attention. Two men were fighting, one from his people and one from Fir'awn's. When asked for help, he struck the other man with his fist and {trap}the man died{/trap}. Musa immediately named it {idea}Shaytan's doing{/idea}.
now: Someone insults your brother in the car park and you step in hot. A shove becomes something worse. {trap}Taking a side in a fight you do not understand{/trap} can wreck lives in seconds. Musa did not defend it; he called it what it was.
old: If I was defending my side, what I did was justified.
new: Anger in a moment of loyalty can still be Shaytan's work, and I should say so plainly.
try: Next time you feel heat rising in an argument, step back one pace and breathe before you act.

title: I wronged myself, so forgive me. And He did.
subtitle: The fastest way back after a terrible mistake

row.title: explaining myself
sub: it was not really my fault

then: Right after the blow, Musa turned to Allah: {idea}"My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me."{/idea} No blaming the fight or the other man. {reward}Then He forgave him.{/reward}
now: You snapped at your mother and slammed the door. Your mind starts building the case for why you were right. {idea}Musa's words are shorter: I did wrong, forgive me.{/idea} Allah answers that kind of honesty.
old: What I did is too serious to be forgiven.
new: Owning my wrong and asking Allah plainly is the door, and He is quick to open it.
try: Tonight, name one wrong to Allah in your own words, with no excuse attached, and ask forgiveness.

title: Never again will I back the wrongdoers.
subtitle: Turning forgiveness into a promise
then: Ibn Kathir explains the favor as {reward}the prestige, power and blessings{/reward} Allah had given Musa. Because of that, Musa vowed he would {idea}never again be a helper of the criminals{/idea}, those who go against Allah's commands.
now: Your skills, your login access, your influence in the group chat. They can be lent to someone else's wrong without you noticing. {idea}Forgiveness is the moment to decide whose side your gifts are on.{/idea}
old: My abilities are mine to use however people ask.
new: Every favor Allah gave me is a reason never to put it at the service of wrong.
try: Think of one thing you are good at. Decide one thing you will never use it for.

title: The same man, the same fight, the next day.
subtitle: When someone keeps pulling you into trouble
then: Musa spent the day {trap}afraid, watching for the consequences{/trap}. Then the same man who had asked for help was fighting another Copt and called him again. Musa told him plainly: {idea}you are clearly misleading{/idea}.
now: The cousin who always has a new fight and always needs you to back him. The friend whose drama you keep getting dragged into. {idea}Sometimes the kind thing is to name the pattern{/idea}, not to jump in again.
old: If someone on my side calls for help, I have to answer.
new: Loyalty does not mean following someone into the same trouble every day.
try: Think of one person who keeps pulling you into conflict. Decide calmly what you will say next time.

title: A frightened man blurted out the secret.
subtitle: How a hidden mistake came to light
then: Musa moved toward the Copt, but the Israelite, {trap}out of cowardice and weakness{/trap}, thought Musa meant to hit him. He cried out about yesterday's killing. Only the two of them had known. The Copt carried the news to Fir'awn, who {trap}resolved to kill Musa{/trap}.
now: You covered for a friend once, and now in a panic they throw your name into the room. {idea}Fear makes people say things they never meant to.{/idea} Be careful whose secrets you share, and how you act when you are scared.
old: The people I helped will always protect me.
new: Fear can turn anyone careless, so I should guard my own conduct before relying on others.
try: Next time you feel cornered, say nothing for ten seconds before you speak.

title: One man ran across the city to warn him.
subtitle: The courage to take a different route
then: Fir'awn's chiefs were {trap}taking counsel together to kill Musa{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says this person is called a man because {idea}he had the courage to take a different route{/idea}, shorter than the pursuers, and reached Musa first with sincere advice.
now: You overhear the plan in the office to blame someone for a failure. You could say nothing. {idea}Or you could be the person who runs ahead{/idea} and quietly warns them. That takes courage, not power.
old: If I overhear something unfair, it is safer to stay out of it.
new: Sincere advice, given at risk, can be the turning point of someone else's life.
try: If you know something a friend needs to hear for their good, tell them kindly today.

title: Alone, afraid, and praying while he walked.
subtitle: Leaving everything with one short dua
then: Musa left Egypt on his own. Ibn Kathir notes {trap}he was not used to being alone{/trap}; he had lived in luxury and leadership. He walked out fearful, watching behind him, and asked {idea}"My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people."{/idea}
now: You leave a job, a marriage, a home, and drive away with everything in the back seat. Your hands are shaking. {idea}You do not have to feel brave to pray.{/idea} Fear and dua can sit in the same breath.
old: If I am this afraid, my faith must be weak.
new: Even a prophet walked away afraid; the point is to turn to Allah while afraid.
try: Memorise Musa's short dua and say it the next time you walk into something scary.

title: No map, just hope that his Lord would guide him.
subtitle: Setting out without knowing the way
then: Turning toward Madyan, Musa said {idea}"Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way."{/idea} Ibn Kathir says Allah did exactly that: He guided him to the straight path in this world and the Hereafter, and made him {reward}guided and a guide for others{/reward}.
now: First day in a new country. The bus map makes no sense, the language is strange, and you are not sure the move was right. {idea}Hope in Allah's guidance is a way to start walking{/idea}, even before the road is clear.
old: I cannot start until I know exactly where this leads.
new: I can set out with hope that my Lord will guide me as I go.
try: Before your next uncertain step, say: perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way.

title: Tired and hunted, he still noticed two women waiting.
subtitle: Seeing the people pushed to the side

row.title: my own problems
sub: I am the one in trouble

then: Musa reached the well of Madyan. Shepherds were watering their flocks while two women {trap}held their sheep back{/trap} so no harm would come to them. Ibn Kathir says {idea}he felt sorry for them and took pity{/idea}, and asked what was wrong.
now: You are stressed, broke, and exhausted, in the supermarket queue. An elderly man is struggling with his bags behind everyone. {idea}Musa had far more reason to look away{/idea}, and he still asked.
old: When my own life is falling apart, I have nothing to give.
new: Even at my lowest, I can notice the person being pushed aside and ask if they are okay.
try: Today, notice one person waiting at the edge of a crowd and offer help.

title: He helped, then sat in the shade and asked.
subtitle: The dua of someone with nothing left
then: Musa watered the flocks for the women, then went back to the shade. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and As-Suddi said he sat beneath a tree. There, with no home and no food, he said: {reward}"My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me."{/reward}
now: You helped your neighbour move, and you go home to an empty fridge and a rent reminder. {idea}You did not ask them for anything. Ask Allah instead.{/idea} Admitting you are in need is not weakness; it is the dua.
old: I should not ask Allah for small things like food or work.
new: Telling Allah plainly that I need any good He sends is exactly what Musa did.
try: Sit somewhere quiet today and tell Allah, in your own words, one thing you need.

title: The answer came walking shyly, with an invitation.
subtitle: Dua answered, and the fear finally lifted
then: When the sisters returned early, their father asked why, and sent one to call Musa. Umar described her as walking shyly, covering herself. Ibn Kathir notes {idea}her good manners{/idea}: she framed it as her father's invitation. Musa told his story and the old man said {reward}"Fear not. You have escaped."{/reward}
now: You prayed under the tree, and the reply comes as a text from someone you barely know: come by, my dad wants to thank you. {reward}Answers often arrive through ordinary people.{/reward} And sometimes the best answer is just someone saying you are safe now.
old: My dua was too small for Allah to answer so quickly.
new: Allah can answer a dua within the hour, through a person I never expected.
try: Look back at today and find one small thing that might have been an answer to a dua.

title: Hire the strong one who can be trusted.
subtitle: Two qualities worth looking for
then: One daughter told her father to hire Musa. Asked how she knew, she said {reward}he lifted a rock that only ten men could lift{/reward}, and on the walk he asked her to walk behind him and guide him. Ibn Mas'ud counted her among the three people with the sharpest discernment.
now: You are choosing a business partner, a flatmate, someone to marry. The talented one and the kind one are not always the same person. {idea}Look for both: able to do the job, and safe to trust.{/idea}
old: Skill is what matters when choosing someone to work with.
new: The best person to rely on has strength and trustworthiness together.
try: Ask yourself honestly which of the two, strength or trust, you need to grow in. Do one thing for it.

title: An offer of marriage, made without pressure.
subtitle: Eight years, or ten if you choose
then: The old man offered Musa marriage to one of his daughters if he tended the flocks for eight years, with two more {reward}as a favor, if he wished{/reward}. He added {idea}"I do not wish to put you in difficulty."{/idea} Musa was a fugitive with nothing; the father did not exploit that.
now: You are hiring someone desperate for work, or renting a room to a student far from home. You could push the terms. {idea}This father chose fairness and ease{/idea} with a man who had no bargaining power.
old: When someone needs me more than I need them, I can set the terms.
new: Dealing fairly and without pressure with someone vulnerable is what the righteous do.
try: In your next deal or request, make one part easier for the other person than it has to be.

title: Agreed, and Allah is witness to our word.
subtitle: A promise kept, and kept generously
then: Musa agreed and put the deal under {idea}Allah as witness{/idea}. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Abbas, recorded by Al-Bukhari, that Musa {reward}fulfilled the longer and better term{/reward}, for when a Messenger of Allah said he would do a thing, he did it.
now: The contract says forty hours; the handshake said you would see the project through. {reward}Musa did the extra, not because he had to.{/reward} Treat your word as something Allah is watching over.
old: Once I have met the minimum, I have done my part.
new: With Allah as witness to my word, I can keep promises fully and even generously.
try: Pick one promise you made recently and finish it a little better than you said you would.

title: He went for warmth and came back with a mission.
subtitle: A cold night, a lost family, a distant fire
then: After completing the longer term, Musa set out with his family to visit his homeland in secret. They said it was {trap}a cold, dark, rainy night{/trap}; they had lost their way and he could not start a fire. Then he saw a fire far off and went toward it, hoping for {reward}directions or a burning stick{/reward}.
now: Your car breaks down on a dark road and your kids are cold in the back. You walk toward the one light you can see, just hoping for a phone signal. {idea}Sometimes the most ordinary need leads you to the biggest turning point of your life.{/idea}
old: Small, practical needs have nothing to do with my spiritual life.
new: Allah can meet me on the way to something as simple as finding warmth for my family.
try: Next time you go out to meet a practical need for your family, make a short dua as you leave.

title: From a tree in a blessed valley: I am Allah.
subtitle: The moment Musa is spoken to
then: Musa found the fire burning in {idea}a green bush{/idea} on the side of the mountain and stood there amazed. Then he was called from the right side of the valley, in a blessed place: {idea}"O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."{/idea}
now: You came to the mosque just to drop off your father, or opened the Quran only to check a reference. {idea}A verse speaks straight to you.{/idea} The One addressing you is not a voice in your head; it is the Lord of everything.
old: Reading the Quran is reading about Allah.
new: When I read it, the Lord of the worlds is addressing me directly.
try: Read one page of the Quran today and imagine each line is addressed to you by name.

title: He ran from the snake, and was called back.
subtitle: Come near, do not fear, you are safe
then: Allah told Musa to throw down the staff he leaned on every day. It moved like a snake and {trap}he turned and fled{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says this is human nature. When Allah said {reward}"Approach and fear not, you are of the secure"{/reward}, he came back to his place.
now: You flinched. You ran from the hard conversation, the diagnosis, the new role. That does not disqualify you. {reward}The call is: come back, you are safe with Me.{/reward}
old: Because I ran from something scary, I have already failed.
new: Running in fear is human; what matters is coming back when Allah calls.
try: Think of one thing you ran from. Take one small step back toward it today.

title: A shining hand, and a way to calm the fear.
subtitle: Two proofs, and a gesture for a frightened heart

key.label: What he was given for fear

then: His hand came out {reward}shining white, with no disease{/reward}. He was also told to draw his arm close to his side to be free from fear. Ibn Kathir suggests that perhaps if a person {idea}puts his hand over his heart{/idea}, following Musa, fear may lessen, if Allah wills.
now: Your chest tightens before the interview, the exam, the phone call from the hospital. {idea}Musa was sent to Fir'awn with a way to steady himself{/idea}, not with a promise that he would never be scared.
old: If I am truly called to something, I should not feel afraid.
new: Allah sends people into hard places and gives them ways to carry their fear.
try: When fear rises today, place your hand over your heart and say: in Allah I place my trust.

title: He told Allah his fear honestly.
subtitle: I killed one of them, and I am afraid
then: Allah commanded Musa to go to Fir'awn, the very man {trap}whose vengeance he had fled{/trap}. Musa did not refuse. He simply told his Lord the truth: {idea}"I killed one of them, and I fear they will kill me."{/idea}
now: You are asked to go back to the place where you messed up: the old workplace, the family you fell out with. Your past is waiting there. {idea}You can tell Allah exactly what scares you{/idea} before you go.
old: I should not tell Allah I am afraid of what He asks of me.
new: Musa named his past and his fear to Allah plainly, and that honesty was the first step.
try: Tell Allah, in your own words, one fear you have not said out loud to anyone.

title: Send my brother with me. He speaks better.
subtitle: Asking for help is not weakness
then: Ibn Kathir says Musa {trap}found it difficult to speak clearly{/trap}. Facing an arrogant, stubborn king, he asked for his brother Harun as a helper, because {idea}the word of two carries more weight than the word of one{/idea}.
now: You are great with spreadsheets and terrible at presentations. You are asked to pitch to the board. {idea}Ask the colleague who explains things well to stand with you.{/idea} Knowing what you cannot do well is wisdom.
old: If I need help, it means I am not good enough.
new: Asking for the right helper is how a prophet faced the hardest task of his life.
try: Name one task where you need someone else's strength, and ask them for help this week.

title: Your brother will strengthen your arm.
subtitle: The request granted, and more besides

key.label: What he did for his brother

then: Allah granted it: {reward}"We will strengthen your arm through your brother."{/reward} One of the early scholars said no one ever did a greater favor for his brother than Musa did for Harun, interceding until he was made a Prophet. Ibn Kathir links the promise of victory to {idea}"It is I and My Messengers who shall be victorious"{/idea}.
now: You got the promotion, and you put your colleague's name forward too. You got into the course and told your little sister how to apply. {reward}Lifting a sibling up with you{/reward} is one of the best things you can ask for.
old: When I succeed, it is my success alone.
new: The best requests carry someone else up with me.
try: Make dua today for a brother, sister or friend by name, asking for something good for them.

title: They saw the signs and called them magic.
subtitle: When the truth is new, it gets dismissed
then: Musa and Harun showed Fir'awn and his chiefs clear miracles. Ibn Kathir says they {trap}realized it was from Allah{/trap} but answered with stubbornness: it is magic, and our forefathers never did this. The problem was not evidence; it was pride.
now: Someone shows you, kindly, that a habit of yours is hurting people. You say they are exaggerating, and anyway "this is how my family always did it." {trap}Two excuses, same as theirs.{/trap}
old: If it is not how I was raised, it must be wrong.
new: "We never did it this way" is not an argument against the truth.
try: Think of one thing you resist only because it is unfamiliar. Look at it again honestly.

title: My Lord knows best who brought guidance.
subtitle: Leaving the verdict with Allah
then: Called a magician, Musa did not trade insults. He said {idea}"My Lord knows best who has come with guidance"{/idea}, and He will decide between us. Ibn Kathir explains the good end as being supported and prevailing.
now: The comment thread is getting ugly. Your relative is twisting your words in the family chat. You want the last word. {idea}You can state the truth once, calmly, and leave the verdict with Allah.{/idea}
old: If I do not win this argument, the truth loses.
new: I can say what is true and let Allah, who knows best, decide the outcome.
try: In your next heated argument, say your point once, then stop replying.

title: Build me a tower so I can look for Musa's God.
subtitle: Mockery dressed up as investigation
then: Fir'awn told his chiefs he knew of {trap}no god for them but himself{/trap}. Ibn Kathir notes he fooled his people and they obeyed him. He ordered Haman to bake bricks and build a towering structure, to show his people that Musa was lying.
now: Sometimes you "look into" something only to prove it wrong. You search for the one article that agrees with you and share it loudly. {trap}That is a tower, not a question.{/trap}
old: I am just asking questions.
new: Building a case to mock the truth is not the same as honestly seeking it.
try: On one topic you have strong opinions about, read the best argument on the other side today.

title: Arrogant, because they thought they would never return.
subtitle: What forgetting the return does to a person
then: Fir'awn and his armies were {trap}arrogant oppressors who spread much mischief{/trap}. Ibn Kathir explains the cause: {trap}they believed there would be no Resurrection{/trap}. With no return in mind, nothing held them back.
now: You notice it in yourself when no one is checking: the extra minutes taken, the rude reply to a delivery driver you will never see again. {idea}Remembering that you return to Allah{/idea} changes how you treat people with less power.
old: What I do where no one sees me does not really count.
new: Remembering I will return to Allah keeps me from acting like I answer to no one.
try: Today, treat one person who has no power over you with extra respect.

title: The whole army, gone in a single morning.
subtitle: See how the wrongdoers ended
then: After all the arrogance and the tower, Allah seized Fir'awn and his soldiers. Ibn Kathir says they were {trap}drowned in a single morning, and not one was left{/trap}. The verse turns to the listener: {idea}see how the wrongdoers ended{/idea}.
now: You watch someone at work rise by stepping on people, and it seems to pay. {idea}This verse says: wait and look at the ending.{/idea} And look at your own small ways of stepping on others.
old: Wrongdoers seem to get away with it.
new: The verse asks me to look at the end of wrongdoing, starting with my own.
try: Think of one small unfairness you have been getting away with. Put it right today.

title: Leaders, but leading the way to the Fire.
subtitle: What kind of example you set
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Fir'awn and his chiefs became {trap}leaders for everyone who followed the same path{/trap}, rejecting the Messengers. Their humiliation in this world is joined to their humiliation in the Hereafter, where {trap}they will not be helped{/trap}.
now: Your younger cousins copy how you talk about people. Your team copies how you cut corners. You are leading someone somewhere. {idea}The question is where.{/idea}
old: I am not a leader, so my example does not matter.
new: Everyone leads someone, and Allah asks where my example takes them.
try: Think of one person who watches you. Do one thing today you would be happy for them to copy.

title: Remembered with a curse, here and on the Day.
subtitle: How a name lives on after its owner
then: Fir'awn built the tallest tower to make his name. Instead, Allah decreed that {trap}a curse would follow them in this world{/trap}, from the Prophets and the believers. Qatadah linked it to {trap}"pursued by a curse in this life and on the Day"{/trap}.
now: Think about how people speak of someone after they leave the job or the family. Not their title, not their car. {idea}What they did to people is what stays.{/idea} You are writing that sentence now.
old: Being powerful is how I will be remembered.
new: What follows me after I am gone is the way I treated people, not what I built.
try: Imagine one sentence people would say about you if you left today. Do one thing to make it kinder.

title: After the ruins came a Book of light.
subtitle: Guidance given so people would remember

row.title: rules to follow
sub: a list of dos and don'ts

then: After Fir'awn and his chiefs were destroyed, Allah revealed {reward}the Tawrah to Musa{/reward}. Ibn Kathir explains it as guidance out of blindness and error, and {idea}a mercy that shows the way to righteous deeds{/idea}, so that people would be reminded.
now: You have been through a hard year: a breakup, a job loss, a scare. Afterwards, what you need is not more noise but {idea}a clear light to walk by{/idea}. That is what Allah gives after the ruins.
old: Scripture is mostly rules and warnings.
new: Allah's Book is light and mercy, given so I can see where to walk and remember Him.
try: Read a short passage of the Quran today looking only for one thing that gives you light.

title: You were not there, yet you told it exactly.
subtitle: How the Prophet ﷺ knew Musa's story

row.title: revelation
sub: as if hearing and seeing it

then: Having told Musa's story from start to end, Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ that he {idea}was not on the western side of the mount{/idea}. Ibn Kathir notes he could not read books and grew up among people who knew nothing of this. Similar lines come after the stories of Maryam and Nuh.
now: You have just read the whole story of Musa in this surah, detail after detail. {idea}Pause on who delivered it{/idea}: a man in Makkah who never sat with historians, telling it as if he had been there.
old: The Quran's stories are just retellings of older ones.
new: The Prophet ﷺ told these events as an eyewitness would, and that itself points to Allah as their source.
try: Think of one detail from Musa's story that moved you, and say a salawat on the Prophet ﷺ who brought it.

title: Long ages passed, so Allah kept sending messengers.
subtitle: Why reminders are needed again
then: Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}people had forgotten the evidence{/trap} Allah established through earlier Prophets. The Prophet ﷺ never lived among the people of Madyan reciting to them, yet told of Shu'ayb. {idea}It is Allah who kept sending.{/idea}
now: You came back from Hajj or Ramadan glowing. Six months later, the glow is gone and old habits are back. {idea}Forgetting over time is human.{/idea} That is why Allah keeps sending reminders, and why you need to keep returning to them.
old: I learned this once, so I do not need reminding.
new: Long stretches of time wear down memory, so I need Allah's reminders again and again.
try: Set one weekly reminder on your phone to read a short surah you already know.

title: Not a witness at the mount, but sent as mercy.
subtitle: A warner for a people who had none
then: Qatadah said the call at Tur refers to Allah calling Musa. The Prophet ﷺ was not there, but Allah revealed it to him {reward}as a mercy to him and to His servants{/reward}, sent to Arabs who {idea}had no warner before him{/idea}.
now: A friend texts you, "Are you sure about this?" before you sign the loan. It annoys you. Later you realise it saved you. {reward}A warning from someone who cares is a mercy.{/reward}
old: Warnings are a burden and a downer.
new: Allah sending a warner is itself a mercy, so I would not walk into harm unaware.
try: Thank one person this week who once warned you away from a mistake.

title: So no one could say: nobody ever told us.
subtitle: Removing the last excuse
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the Prophet ﷺ was sent {idea}to establish proof and leave no excuse{/idea}, so that no one could say no warner ever came. He links it to {idea}"so that mankind should have no plea against Allah after the Messengers"{/idea}.
now: You know the Quran is on the shelf. You know the app is on your phone. {idea}"No one ever told me" is not really available to you anymore.{/idea} That is not a threat. It is an invitation that has already arrived.
old: If I never really looked into it, I cannot be blamed.
new: The message has already reached me, so the question now is what I do with it.
try: Open the Quran today and read one passage you have never read before.

title: Give us Musa's miracles, they said, then rejected those too.
subtitle: When no amount of proof is enough
then: When truth came, the Makkans asked {trap}why he was not given what Musa was given{/trap}: the staff, the hand, the parting sea. Yet Fir'awn saw all of that and still denied. Then they called both {trap}"two works of magic supporting each other"{/trap} and rejected them together.
now: You tell yourself you will start praying once you understand everything. Then you understand, and you need one more answer. {trap}The goalpost keeps moving.{/trap} Notice when a question is really a delay.
old: I will believe properly once I get the right sign.
new: If every proof gets a new excuse, the problem is not the proof.
try: Name one excuse you keep giving for a good habit. Do the habit once today anyway.

title: Bring a better guide, and I will follow it.
subtitle: An open challenge to the doubters
then: Ibn Abbas said the "two" here are {idea}the Tawrah and the Quran{/idea}, which Allah often mentions together. The Prophet ﷺ was told to answer: then {idea}bring a Book from Allah that guides better{/idea}, and I will follow it.
now: Your friend mocks your faith at dinner. Fair enough, you might say: what do you live by that guides you better? {idea}Criticism is easy. Offering a better path is harder.{/idea}
old: If people criticise my faith, I have to win every point.
new: I can calmly ask what better guidance they have to offer.
try: Write down three ways the Quran has guided a decision of yours. Keep the list.

title: No answer means they only follow their desires.
subtitle: The real reason behind refusing
then: If they could not answer, Ibn Kathir says, it showed they {trap}follow their own desires with no basis or evidence{/trap}. The verse asks: who is more astray than one who follows desire {idea}without guidance from Allah{/idea}?
now: You decide to skip the hard conversation, then find reasons it is the wise choice. You want the thing, then build the argument. {trap}Desire first, logic afterwards.{/trap} Notice the order in your own head.
old: My choices are based on careful reasoning.
new: Often I follow what I want and dress it up as reasoning, unless I check it against Allah's guidance.
try: Before one decision today, ask: is this what I want, or what is right? Answer honestly.

title: Word after word, so they might remember.
subtitle: A message conveyed piece by piece
then: Mujahid said this means {idea}"We have explained the Word to them"{/idea}, and that it was addressed to Quraysh. Qatadah said Allah told them what He did in the past and what He will do in the future, {reward}that they might remember{/reward}.
now: Your mother has told you the same thing a hundred times: call your grandmother. One day it finally lands. {idea}Repeated reminders are a sign someone has not given up on you.{/idea}
old: If I have heard a reminder before, it has nothing new for me.
new: Allah repeats His message out of care, waiting for the day it sinks in.
try: Pick one reminder you have heard many times and act on it once today.

title: Those who knew the earlier Book recognised this one.
subtitle: People who heard the Quran and believed
then: Sa'id bin Jubayr said this was revealed about seventy priests sent by An-Najashi. The Prophet ﷺ recited Surah Ya Sin to them; {reward}they began to weep and embraced Islam{/reward}.
now: You have studied something deeply, and then someone shows you a truth that fits what you already know. {idea}Real knowledge makes you quicker to recognise truth, not slower.{/idea} Let what you know make you humble, not defensive.
old: The more I know, the harder it is for anyone to teach me.
new: Sincere knowledge prepares the heart to recognise truth when it arrives.
try: Listen to someone today with the aim of learning one thing, not of correcting them.

title: We were already submitting before it came.
subtitle: When a new truth completes an old faith
then: When the Quran was recited to them they said {idea}"It is the truth from our Lord."{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains their words: even before it came, {reward}they believed in One God and responded sincerely to His commands{/reward}.
now: You grew up praying, but only now do you understand what you say. It is not a new religion; {idea}it is the same submission, finally seen clearly{/idea}. Every return to Allah builds on what came before.
old: Growing in faith means my past practice did not count.
new: Sincere submission before now is what makes it easy to say yes when the truth becomes clear.
try: Thank Allah for one good habit you learned as a child that still holds you today.

title: Double reward for patience and answering evil with good.
subtitle: Three habits that earn twice
then: Ibn Kathir explains they are patient because {idea}holding to the truth is not easy{/idea}. He cites the hadith in the Sahih that three are given their reward twice, including a person of the Book who believed in his Prophet and then in Muhammad ﷺ. They {reward}repel evil with good{/reward}.
now: A colleague takes credit for your work in the meeting. Your sibling says something cutting at Eid. You could hit back. {reward}Or you could answer with a good word and move on.{/reward} That choice is what the verse rewards.
old: If someone wrongs me, a fair response is to wrong them back.
new: Answering wrong with good, patiently, is what earns a double reward.
try: Next time someone is unkind to you today, reply with one genuinely kind sentence.

title: Peace be upon you. We are not here to argue.
subtitle: Walking away from ugly talk with dignity
then: When foolish people spoke to them foolishly, Ibn Kathir says, {idea}they turned away and did not respond in kind{/idea}. They said: to us our deeds, to you yours, peace be upon you. He links it to passing by vain talk {reward}with dignity{/reward}.
now: The comments under your post turn nasty. The uncle at the wedding starts in on you again. {idea}You can say "peace be with you" and leave the thread.{/idea} Not every insult needs your reply.
old: If I do not answer back, I look weak.
new: Walking away from ugly talk with a word of peace is strength, not weakness.
try: Leave one argument today, online or offline, with a calm word and no reply after it.

title: You cannot guide even those you love most.
subtitle: Guidance belongs to Allah alone
then: Recorded in the Two Sahihs: this was revealed about Abu Talib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle who protected and loved him. On his deathbed the Prophet ﷺ kept urging him to say La ilaha illallah, but {trap}he refused{/trap}. Allah told His Messenger ﷺ that {idea}guidance is not in your hands{/idea}.
now: Your father, your brother, your best friend from school. You have prayed and talked and hoped for years. {idea}Your part is to love them and convey it well.{/idea} The opening of a heart belongs to Allah, not to you.
old: If someone I love does not change, I have failed them.
new: Even the Prophet ﷺ could not guide his beloved uncle; my part is to convey, and Allah guides.
try: Make dua for one person you wish would come closer to Allah, and let go of the pressure.

title: Afraid of losing their safety, inside a safe sanctuary.
subtitle: The excuse that ignores where safety comes from
then: Some Makkans said that if they followed the guidance, {trap}the pagan tribes around them would attack{/trap}. Allah answered: did We not give them {reward}a secure sanctuary{/reward}, with fruits brought from Ta'if and beyond? It was safe while they worshipped idols; why not when they follow the truth?
now: You do not pray at work because your colleagues might think you strange and your career might stall. {idea}The job, the salary, the safe flat you live in already came from Allah.{/idea} He does not take away safety for obeying Him.
old: If I openly practise my faith, I will lose my security.
new: The safety I fear losing was given by Allah, who will not abandon me for following Him.
try: Do one small act of faith openly today that you usually hide out of worry.

title: Comfortable towns, ungrateful for their comfort, now empty.
subtitle: When ease turns into arrogance

key.label: Who owns it in the end

then: Addressing the people of Makkah, Allah points to towns that {trap}denied the blessing of ample provision{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says their land became empty; you can see nothing but their dwellings. He compares it to the example of {idea}a township secure and content{/idea} that turned ungrateful.
now: A full fridge, a car that starts, a salary that lands every month. It is easy to stop noticing, then to feel entitled. {trap}Comfort without gratitude is how the slide begins.{/trap}
old: My comfortable life is simply what I have earned.
new: Ease is a blessing to thank Allah for, and it can be taken when it breeds arrogance.
try: Before your next meal, name three blessings in the room and thank Allah for each.

title: No town is destroyed before a messenger reaches it.
subtitle: Allah's justice comes before His punishment
then: Ibn Kathir says this shows {idea}Allah's justice: He destroys no one unjustly{/idea}. The "mother town" is Makkah, and the Prophet ﷺ was sent from it to all people, Arab and non-Arab. He cites the hadith in the Two Sahihs: {idea}"I have been sent to the red and the black."{/idea}
now: You feel like life is ambushing you. But look back: the reminders came first. The friend's advice, the verse in Friday's khutbah. {idea}Allah warns before He holds anyone to account.{/idea} That is a mercy, and an invitation to listen now.
old: Allah punishes people without warning.
new: Allah always sends a reminder first and only holds the wrongdoers to account.
try: Think of one reminder you have received lately. Act on one small part of it today.

title: Everything you have is decoration for a short life.
subtitle: What lasts versus what shines
then: Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ: {idea}this world compared to the Hereafter is as if one of you dipped his finger in the sea; let him see what comes back{/idea}. The verse ends by asking those who prefer this world: {trap}will you not use reason?{/trap}
now: You save for months for the new phone. Two years later it is in a drawer, slow and scratched. {idea}Look at what is on your finger, and then at the sea.{/idea} Enjoy what you have, but do not trade the lasting for it.
old: The things I own now are what really matter.
new: What I have is a short enjoyment; what is with Allah is better and lasts.
try: Before your next purchase, pause and give a small amount in charity first.

title: A promise kept, or a few days of luxury?
subtitle: Two lives that only look similar
then: Ibn Kathir explains the comparison: the one who believes in Allah's promise for righteous deeds, {reward}which he will undoubtedly attain{/reward}, against the one who {trap}enjoys a few days in this life{/trap} while denying the meeting with Allah. Mujahid narrated it was revealed about specific Makkans; Ibn Kathir says the meaning is more general.
now: Two colleagues earn the same, drive similar cars, scroll the same apps. One quietly gives, prays, keeps promises. {idea}From outside they look alike. The endings will not be.{/idea}
old: As long as my life looks good, it does not matter what I live for.
new: Two similar-looking lives can lead to very different endings, depending on what I trust.
try: Do one thing today only because Allah promised a reward for it.

title: Where are the partners you used to claim?
subtitle: A question that will be asked one day
then: Ibn Kathir describes this as a rebuke: {trap}where are the gods you worshipped in the world? Can they help you?{/trap} He links it to the verse where people come before Allah {idea}alone, as He created them{/idea}, all they claimed having vanished.
now: You may not bow to statues, but you might lean on things the same way: your boss's approval, your followers, your savings. {idea}Ask what you are treating as your rescuer.{/idea} Then ask whether it will be there when you need it most.
old: Idolatry is about statues, so it has nothing to do with me.
new: Anything I rely on instead of Allah is a partner that will not answer when it matters.
try: Name one thing you rely on more than Allah. Hand that worry to Him in a short dua.

title: The ones who misled you will disown you.
subtitle: When leaders and followers turn on each other
then: Ibn Kathir says these are the devils and those who called people to disbelief. They will {trap}testify against their followers and declare their innocence{/trap}. He cites Ibrahim's words: on the Day of Resurrection {trap}you shall disown each other{/trap}.
now: The friend who said "everyone does it" and talked you into it. The influencer whose advice you followed blindly. {trap}When it goes wrong, they will not stand next to you.{/trap} Choose whose lead you follow with that in mind.
old: The people pushing me toward wrong will share the blame.
new: Those who mislead me will disown me, so I must own my choices now.
try: Think of one voice that pulls you toward wrong. Mute or step back from it this week.

title: They call, and nothing answers. If only they had been guided.
subtitle: A wish that comes too late
then: They will be told to call on their partners to save them, {trap}as they hoped in this world{/trap}. No one answers. Ibn Kathir says when they see the punishment {idea}they will wish they had been among the guided in this world{/idea}.
now: You keep telling yourself you will sort out your prayer after exams, after the wedding, after the promotion. {idea}This verse is the "if only" said too late.{/idea} You still have the chance to say it early.
old: I will take guidance seriously later in life.
new: The wish to have been guided is only useful while I am still alive to act on it.
try: Pick one thing you keep postponing for your faith and do the first small step today.

title: How did you answer the messengers?
subtitle: The second question on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir says the first call is about Tawhid; this one asks {idea}how you dealt with the Messengers sent to you{/idea}. He compares it to the questions in the grave: who is your Lord, who is your Prophet, what is your religion. The believer answers; {trap}the disbeliever says "I do not know"{/trap}.
now: Imagine being asked tonight: how did you respond to the message? Not what you scrolled past, not what you meant to do. {idea}What you actually did with it.{/idea} You are writing that answer this week.
old: Knowing about the Prophet ﷺ is the same as following him.
new: The question will be how I responded to the messengers, not just what I knew.
try: Choose one sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ you know but do not practise, and do it today.

title: Every answer goes blank, and no one can help.
subtitle: No asking around on that Day
then: Mujahid said {trap}the proof will be obscured from them{/trap}, so they cannot ask one another for help by virtue of their blood ties. Ibn Kathir adds: whoever is blind to Allah's signs in this world will be blind in the Hereafter.
now: In the exam hall your mind goes blank, and you cannot lean over to ask your friend. {idea}This is that feeling, but final.{/idea} The only notes you get to bring are the ones you wrote in your life.
old: My family's faith will cover for my own.
new: On that Day no one can whisper me the answer; I need to prepare it now.
try: Spend five quiet minutes today reflecting on what your honest answer would be.

title: But whoever turns back, believes, and does good will succeed.
subtitle: The door still open after the warning
then: After the hard scenes, Allah opens a door: one who repented, believed and did good {reward}will be among the successful{/reward}. Ibn Kathir notes the word "perhaps", when Allah uses it, means {idea}the thing will inevitably come to pass{/idea}, by His grace and mercy.
now: You have read the warnings and feel heavy. You think of the things you have done. {reward}This verse is for you.{/reward} Turn back today, believe, do one good thing. Allah's "perhaps" is a promise.
old: After what I have done, success with Allah is out of reach.
new: Repentance, faith and good deeds lead to success, and Allah's promise of it is sure.
try: Make sincere tawbah tonight for one specific thing, then do one good deed to follow it.

title: He creates what He wills, and He chooses.
subtitle: The choice that is not ours
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah alone {idea}creates and makes decisions{/idea}; no one can dispute with Him or reverse His judgement. What He wills happens and what He does not will does not. He links it to {idea}"It is not for a believer... to have any option"{/idea} once Allah has decreed.
now: You did not choose your parents, your height, the year you were born, the illness that showed up. {idea}Some choices were never yours.{/idea} That can feel like a loss, or a relief: the Wise One chose them.
old: If I did not choose it, it must be a mistake.
new: Allah creates and chooses, and what He chose for me came from His wisdom.
try: Name one thing about your life you did not choose. Say alhamdulillah for it once today.

title: He knows what you hide and what you show.
subtitle: No gap between inside and outside for Allah
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}knows what is hidden in their hearts, just as He knows what they do openly{/idea}. He cites the verse that it is the same whether you conceal speech or declare it, {idea}hidden by night or out by day{/idea}.
now: You smile at the colleague and resent them inside. You give in public, then complain in private. {idea}To Allah there is no backstage.{/idea} That is uncomfortable, and also freeing: you do not have to perform for Him.
old: What I keep inside does not really count.
new: Allah knows my hidden heart exactly as He sees my actions, so I can be honest with Him.
try: Tell Allah one hidden feeling you have not admitted to anyone and ask Him to purify it.

title: His is the praise, first and last, and the decision.
subtitle: Praise in both lives, and the return to Him
then: Ibn Kathir explains: in all that He does, {reward}He is to be praised for His justice and wisdom{/reward}. His decision cannot be put back. Everyone returns to Him on the Day, and {idea}none of their deeds will be concealed{/idea}.
now: You say alhamdulillah after a good meal. Can you say it at the bus stop in the rain, or after the rejection email? {idea}The praise is His in the first life and the last{/idea}, not only in the good moments.
old: I praise Allah when things go my way.
new: All praise belongs to Allah in every situation, because His decisions are just and wise.
try: Say alhamdulillah once today right after something goes wrong.

title: What if the night never ended?
subtitle: Morning light as a gift you never asked for
then: Allah reminds His servants of the night and day, {reward}without which they could not survive{/reward}. Ibn Kathir says continuous night would be harmful, causing {trap}boredom and stress{/trap}. Which god besides Allah could bring the light back?
now: Think of a winter where it is dark when you leave for work and dark when you come home. How heavy that feels. {idea}Every sunrise is something Allah sends{/idea}, not something owed to you.
old: Sunrise is just how nature works.
new: Each morning's light is a mercy only Allah brings.
try: Tomorrow, step outside or open a window at first light and thank Allah for it.

title: And what if the day never stopped?
subtitle: Rest as a gift, not a weakness
then: If the day never ended, Ibn Kathir says, {trap}their bodies would get tired from so much movement and activity{/trap}. Only Allah could bring {reward}a night to rest from your work{/reward}. The verse asks: will you not see?
now: Your laptop is open at midnight. The emails never stop and your phone glows by the bed. {idea}Night is Allah's gift so you can stop.{/idea} Treating rest as laziness is turning down something He made for you.
old: Resting means I am falling behind.
new: Night and rest are mercies from Allah, given so my body can recover.
try: Tonight, put your phone away thirty minutes before sleep and thank Allah for the night.

title: Night to rest, day to earn, both out of mercy.
subtitle: The rhythm of a day as a reason to give thanks

row.title: make it up
sub: in the night, or the day

then: After the two questions about endless night and endless day, Allah says both were made {reward}out of His mercy{/reward}: rest at night, travel and work by day. Ibn Kathir adds that {idea}whoever misses something at night can make it up during the day{/idea}, and the reverse.
now: You slept through Fajr, or the workday ate your plans for Quran. It feels like the day is lost. {idea}The night and day take turns so you can catch up.{/idea} The rhythm itself is a second chance.
old: If I miss a good deed at its time, the chance is gone.
new: Allah made night and day follow each other so I can make up what I missed and thank Him.
try: Make up one missed good habit from earlier today before you sleep tonight.

title: The same question again: where are they now?
subtitle: Asked before every witness on the Day
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {trap}another call by way of rebuke{/trap} for those who worshipped others besides Allah, made {idea}before all the witnesses{/idea}. The question from verse 62 returns, right after the verses about night and day: who else gave you those?
now: You just read that Allah alone brings morning and night. Now the question returns. {idea}Hearing it twice is a gift{/idea}: a second chance to check what you lean on, today, before it is asked for real.
old: I already heard this warning, so it is not for me.
new: Allah repeats the question so I keep checking whom I truly rely on.
try: Before bed, ask yourself honestly: what did I rely on most today, other than Allah?

title: Bring your proof. And every invented claim disappears.
subtitle: A witness from every nation
then: Mujahid said the witness from every nation means {idea}a Messenger{/idea}. Then they are asked for proof of their claim that Allah had partners. Ibn Kathir says {trap}they will not speak and will not find any answer{/trap}; the lies they invented will vanish.
now: You have explanations ready for the things you know are wrong: stress, everyone does it, it is complicated. {idea}Picture saying them in front of Allah.{/idea} If they fade even in your imagination, let them go now.
old: I can always explain my choices if asked.
new: Before Allah only the truth stands, and invented excuses vanish.
try: Pick one excuse you use often and drop it for a day. Do the thing or admit why you do not.

title: So rich his keys were heavy, so proud he oppressed.
subtitle: Qarun, and the advice he was given
then: Ibn Abbas and others said Qarun was {idea}Musa's paternal cousin{/idea}. He was given treasures whose keys a band of strong men could not carry, yet he {trap}behaved arrogantly toward his own people{/trap}. The righteous among them advised him sincerely: do not exult.
now: Your cousin buys a new car and the family chat fills with photos and hints. Or you got the bonus and you cannot stop mentioning it. {trap}Wealth can make you look down on your own people.{/trap} Notice the urge to show off.
old: If I have more, I have the right to show it off.
new: Allah does not love those who gloat, so wealth calls for humility, not display.
try: Next time you want to post or mention something you bought, pause and skip it.

title: Use it for the Hereafter, enjoy your share, be generous.
subtitle: The best financial advice ever given

row.title: do good
sub: as Allah did good to you

then: His people told Qarun to {idea}use his wealth to draw closer to his Lord{/idea}, and not forget his lawful share: food, drink, clothing, home, family. Ibn Kathir: your Lord, your self, your family and your visitors {reward}each have rights over you{/reward}. Be generous as Allah was generous to you.
now: Payday arrives. Rent, a meal out with your family, a transfer to your mother, something to the food bank. {idea}That is this verse in a banking app.{/idea} Not guilt about enjoying it, not forgetting where it came from.
old: Being religious means feeling guilty about enjoying money.
new: I can enjoy my lawful share while using what Allah gave me for the Hereafter and for others.
try: On your next payday, set aside one small amount for someone in need before anything else.

title: I earned this myself, he said.
subtitle: Mistaking a gift for proof you deserve it

row.title: Allah loves me
sub: or He would not give it

then: Qarun answered his advisers: {trap}"I was only given it because of knowledge I have."{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: Allah gave me this because He knows I deserve it. He notes this is what people of little knowledge say when they see someone wealthy. Many before him were {trap}stronger and richer{/trap}, and were destroyed.
now: You worked hard, studied, took the risk, and it paid off. It is tempting to think: I made this happen, and that is why I have it. {idea}The skill, the health, the timing were all given.{/idea}
old: I have what I have because I earned it and deserve it.
new: My success is Allah's gift and a test, not proof that I am better.
try: Name one thing you are proud of achieving. List three things Allah gave you that made it possible.

title: He paraded his wealth, and the crowd wished for it.
subtitle: Envy at the procession
then: Qarun went out before his people in all his splendor: {trap}fine clothes, fine horses, servants and retinue{/trap}. Those whose desires were for the world said {trap}"if only we had what Qarun has"{/trap}, calling him very lucky.
now: Holiday photos, a friend's new kitchen, an influencer's car. You scroll and feel smaller. {trap}Your own life starts to look poor.{/trap} That feeling is the crowd at Qarun's parade.
old: People with more than me are the lucky ones.
new: Envying someone's display shows where my own heart is pointed.
try: When envy hits while scrolling today, close the app and thank Allah for one thing you have.

title: Allah's reward is better, and only the patient reach it.
subtitle: What people of knowledge said at the parade

row.title: the patient
sub: who let go of the craving

then: People of beneficial knowledge answered the crowd: {reward}Allah's reward is better for those who believe and do good{/reward}. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith that Allah has prepared what no eye has seen and no ear has heard. Ibn Jarir said it is reached by {idea}those who patiently give up love of this world{/idea}.
now: Your friend posts the new car; you post nothing, saving for your parents' care. It does not look like winning. {reward}What Allah has prepared is beyond what anyone can see.{/reward} Patience with your own life is the price.
old: If I cannot have it now, I am missing out.
new: Patiently not chasing this world is the way to a reward far better than any parade.
try: Tell one friend something kind about their life today instead of comparing it to yours.

title: The earth swallowed him, and no one could help.
subtitle: What his wealth and servants could not do
then: After his pride and transgression against his people, {trap}Qarun and his dwelling were swallowed by the earth{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says his wealth, servants and retinue {trap}could not protect him{/trap}. He also cites hadith in Al-Bukhari and Ahmad about a man who walked in arrogance and was swallowed up.
now: You may have insurance, savings, connections. Good things. {idea}But the verse asks what any of it can do against Allah's decision.{/idea} Hold them lightly, and walk without arrogance.
old: With enough money and the right people, I am protected.
new: No wealth or group can protect anyone from Allah, so humility is my real safety.
try: Walk somewhere today slowly and humbly, making dhikr instead of checking your phone.

title: Yesterday they envied him. Today they were grateful.
subtitle: The crowd learns what wealth does not mean

row.title: His favor
sub: or we would be gone too

then: Those who had wished for his place {idea}began to say that Allah expands and restricts provision as He wills{/idea}. Ibn Kathir says wealth does not show Allah is pleased with its owner, citing Ibn Mas'ud: {reward}Allah gives wealth to those He loves and those He does not, but faith only to those He loves{/reward}.
now: You envied a classmate's life for years. Then you hear what was really going on behind the photos. {idea}Your heart turns to gratitude for what you were spared.{/idea} Faith, not money, is the sign of being loved.
old: Having more money means Allah loves someone more.
new: Allah gives wealth to many, but faith only to those He loves.
try: Thank Allah today for one thing you once wanted and did not get.

title: The final home is for those who seek no rank above others.
subtitle: Humility as the entry ticket
then: Ali said: {trap}if a man wants his sandal straps to be better than his companion's{/trap}, he is one of those meant here. Ibn Kathir explains that the problem is wanting to appear better than others. Simply liking to look good is fine: {reward}"Allah is beautiful and loves beauty."{/reward}
now: You pick the outfit for the wedding. Is it because you like it, or because you need to outshine your cousin? {idea}The verse is not against nice things. It is against wanting to be above people.{/idea}
old: Wanting to look good is the same as arrogance.
new: Liking beauty is fine; wanting to be above others is what closes the door.
try: Before you get dressed or post a photo today, ask: is this for me, or to be above someone?

title: Good returns better; evil returns only as much.
subtitle: Generosity for good, justice for evil
then: Ibn Kathir explains that {reward}Allah's reward is better than the servant's good deed{/reward}, since He multiplies it many times. Evil is repaid only by what was done. He calls this {idea}the position of generosity and justice{/idea}.
now: You helped your neighbour carry the shopping, five minutes of effort. Allah counts it as more than that. You snapped at your child; it is counted as exactly that, no more. {reward}The scale is tilted toward your good.{/reward}
old: My small good deeds hardly count against my mistakes.
new: Allah multiplies every good and counts every wrong only as itself, so good always gains.
try: Do three small good deeds today, each under five minutes.

title: The One who gave you the Quran will bring you back.
subtitle: A promise to the Prophet ﷺ while he faced opposition
then: Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn Abbas said the "return" here means {reward}Makkah{/reward}: He will bring you back as He brought you out. Ibn Abbas also explained it as death, the Day of Resurrection, and Paradise. Ibn Kathir notes the Prophet ﷺ {idea}will be asked about the message entrusted to him{/idea}.
now: You had to leave: a home, a country, a job you loved. It feels like the door shut for good. {reward}The One who gave you your duties can bring you back{/reward}, to that place or to something better.
old: Once I have been pushed out of somewhere, it is over.
new: The One who entrusted me with my task can bring me back, in this life or the next.
try: Make dua today for one place or person you had to leave behind.

title: You never expected the Book. It came as mercy.
subtitle: An unexpected gift, and what follows from it

key.label: What a gift asks of you

row.title: loyalty
sub: do not help what opposes it

then: Ibn Kathir explains that before revelation came, the Prophet ﷺ {idea}did not expect it would be sent to him{/idea}. It was {reward}a mercy to him and to mankind because of him{/reward}. Having received such a blessing, he was told never to be a helper to those rejecting it.
now: You did not ask to be born into a home with the Quran on the shelf. You may have found it later, by surprise. {reward}It is a mercy you never earned.{/reward} The least you can do is not lend your effort to what pulls people away from it.
old: Having the Quran in my life is just how I grew up.
new: The Quran reaching me is an unexpected mercy, and I should not help anything that works against it.
try: Thank Allah today for the specific way the Quran first reached you.

title: Do not let opposition turn you away. Keep inviting.
subtitle: Staying steady when people push back

row.title: their opposition
sub: do not let it stop you

then: Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}do not let their opposition affect you{/idea} or put people off your way; do not worry about it. Allah will make the message prevail. So {idea}invite to your Lord{/idea}, to worship Him alone.
now: You started praying at work and someone made a joke. You shared a verse and got eye-rolls. {idea}Do not let that turn you away from what you know is true.{/idea} Keep going, gently.
old: If people push back, I should keep my faith to myself.
new: Opposition should not turn me from Allah's verses; I keep inviting, gently and steadily.
try: Share one beneficial verse or saying with someone today, kindly and without arguing.

title: Everything perishes except His Face.
subtitle: The last word of the surah
then: The surah that told of Fir'awn's tower and Qarun's treasure ends here. Ibn Kathir says Allah is {idea}Eternal, Ever Living{/idea}; while His creation dies, He never will. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ words that the truest line of a poet was {idea}"everything except Allah is false"{/idea}. To Him all return.
now: Your phone, your job title, the house, the body you look after. All of it is temporary, even the people you love. {idea}Only Allah remains.{/idea} Everything else is worth loving only as a way back to Him.
old: The things I build and own are what will last.
new: Everything perishes except Allah, so the only thing that lasts is what I do for Him.
try: Pick one thing you do every day and add a quiet intention for Allah to it.
